Acronyms 159

AAPM
American Association of Physicists in Medicine. The professional body whose task groups write the display and imaging quality control reports.
ABII
American Board of Imaging Informatics. The board that sets and awards the imaging informatics professional credential.
ACK
Acknowledgment. The HL7 reply message that tells the sender whether a message was received and accepted.
ACR
American College of Radiology. The radiology professional society that publishes practice parameters and runs imaging accreditation programs.
ADT
Admit, Discharge, Transfer. The HL7 message family that carries patient registration, updates, and merges.
AE
Application Entity. A named DICOM endpoint; its AE title identifies the device or application on the network.
AGP
Accelerated Graphics Port. An old graphics card slot you recognize on legacy workstations.
AI
Artificial Intelligence. Software that learns patterns from data, used in imaging to flag or measure findings.
AP
Anteroposterior. A projection in which the x-ray beam enters the front of the body and exits the back.
ARP
Address Resolution Protocol. The protocol that finds the hardware address that goes with an IP address on the local network.
ATNA
Audit Trail and Node Authentication. The IHE profile for central audit logging and encrypted connections between trusted systems.
BC
Business Continuity. The plan for keeping clinical work going while systems are down.
CAD
Computer-Aided Detection. Software that marks areas on an image for the reader to consider, as a second look.
CD
Compact Disc. Portable media still used to hand a patient their images.
CIFS
Common Internet File System. An older name for the Windows file-sharing protocol.
CIIP
Certified Imaging Informatics Professional. The ABII credential for people who run imaging systems: 170 questions in 2 hours 50 minutes.
CIO
Chief Information Officer. The executive who leads information technology for the organization.
CMIO
Chief Medical Informatics Officer. A physician leader who guides how clinical information systems are used.
CPI
Consistent Presentation of Images. The IHE profile that makes grayscale images look the same on every display.
CPT
Current Procedural Terminology. The code set that names medical procedures for billing and reporting.
CPU
Central Processing Unit. The processor that runs a computer's instructions.
CSV
Comma-Separated Values. A plain text file where each row is a record and commas separate the fields.
CT
Computed Tomography. Imaging that builds cross-sectional slices from x-ray measurements.
DAS
Direct-Attached Storage. Drives attached directly to one server and not shared over a storage network.
DHCP
Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol. The service that hands out IP addresses and network settings automatically.
DICOM
Digital Imaging and Communications in Medicine. The standard for image objects, the services that move them, and how devices connect.
DICOMDIR
DICOM Directory. The index file on portable media that lists the studies on the disc or drive.
DMAIC
Define, Measure, Analyze, Improve, Control. The five phases of the Six Sigma improvement method.
DNS
Domain Name System. The service that turns host names into IP addresses.
DR
Disaster Recovery. The plan and technology for restoring systems and data after a major failure.
DVD
Digital Versatile Disc. Higher-capacity optical media sometimes used for large studies.
DXA
Dual-Energy X-ray Absorptiometry. The bone density scan; its measurements can flow into the report as a structured report.
ECG
Electrocardiogram. A recording of the heart's electrical activity, stored in cardiology systems as a waveform.
EHR
Electronic Health Record. The shared digital record of a patient's care across providers and settings.
EMR
Electronic Medical Record. The digital record of a patient's care within one organization.
EOSL
End of Service Life. The date after which the vendor no longer supports a product.
FHIR
Fast Healthcare Interoperability Resources. A web-based standard for exchanging health data as small resources over HTTPS.
FTP
File Transfer Protocol. An older protocol for copying files between computers, with no encryption of its own.
GB
Gigabyte. About one billion bytes; a large CT study can reach a few of them.
GDPR
General Data Protection Regulation. The European privacy law with strict consent and data-subject rights.
GPU
Graphics Processing Unit. The processor that draws images and does 3D rendering.
GSDF
Grayscale Standard Display Function. The DICOM curve that maps pixel values to luminance so equal steps look equal.
HA
High Availability. A design that keeps a service running through the failure of a component.
HIPAA
Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act. The United States law that protects health information and sets safeguards for its use.
HITECH
Health Information Technology for Economic and Clinical Health Act. The law that strengthened HIPAA and added breach notification duties.
HL7
Health Level Seven. The standard for messages that move orders, patient data, and reports between systems.
HTTP
Hypertext Transfer Protocol. The protocol of the web, using port 80 by default.
HTTPS
Hypertext Transfer Protocol Secure. HTTP carried inside TLS encryption, using port 443 by default.
ICD
International Classification of Diseases. The code set for diagnoses and reasons for care.
ID
Identifier. A value that names one patient, order, or object.
IHE
Integrating the Healthcare Enterprise. The initiative that defines profiles describing how standards are used together to solve a workflow problem.
IID
Invoke Image Display. The IHE profile that opens the viewer on the right study from another application.
IOPS
Input/Output Operations Per Second. How many reads and writes a storage system can sustain each second.
IP
Internet Protocol. The addressing protocol that moves packets between networks.
IR
Interventional Radiology. Image-guided procedures done through small openings instead of surgery.
IRB
Institutional Review Board. The committee that reviews research and says what patient data may leave the organization.
iSCSI
Internet Small Computer System Interface. Block storage carried over ordinary TCP and Ethernet.
IT
Information Technology. The department and discipline that runs computers, networks, and servers.
JPEG
Joint Photographic Experts Group. The image compression family behind several DICOM transfer syntaxes.
JSON
JavaScript Object Notation. A lightweight text format for structured data, used by web services.
KIN
Key Image Note. The IHE profile for flagging significant images with a comment.
KPI
Key Performance Indicator. A measured number that shows how well a service is performing.
LAN
Local Area Network. A network inside one building or campus.
LDAP
Lightweight Directory Access Protocol. The protocol for looking up users and groups in a directory, on port 389.
LDAPS
LDAP over TLS. The encrypted form of LDAP, on port 636.
LOINC
Logical Observation Identifiers Names and Codes. The code set for observations and orders, including many laboratory and imaging names.
MAC
Media Access Control. The hardware address of a network card, used by switches to forward frames.
MB
Megabyte. About one million bytes; a single CT slice is about half of one.
MDM
Medical Document Management. The HL7 message family for transcribed or scanned documents and their status.
MLLP
Minimal Lower Layer Protocol. The simple framing that carries an HL7 message over a TCP connection.
MPPS
Modality Performed Procedure Step. The DICOM message in which a modality reports that an exam started, finished, or was stopped.
MQSA
Mammography Quality Standards Act. The United States law that regulates mammography facilities and records.
MRI
Magnetic Resonance Imaging. Imaging that uses a strong magnetic field and radio waves to make slices of the body.
MRN
Medical Record Number. The identifier a facility assigns to one patient across its systems.
MWL
Modality Worklist. The DICOM service that gives a modality its scheduled exams and demographics.
NAS
Network-Attached Storage. Shared file storage reached over the network with SMB or NFS.
NAT
Network Address Translation. A router function that maps private addresses to a public one.
NFS
Network File System. The Unix and Linux protocol for sharing files over a network.
NIC
Network Interface Card. The hardware that connects a computer to the network.
NIST
National Institute of Standards and Technology. The United States standards body whose frameworks guide security controls.
OBX
Observation Result Segment. The HL7 segment that carries one result value, such as a line of report text.
OMI
Imaging Order Message. The newer HL7 message type for imaging orders.
ORM
Order Message. The HL7 message that carries a new, changed, or cancelled order.
ORU
Observation Result Unsolicited. The HL7 message that carries a report or result to the record.
OS
Operating System. The base software that runs a computer, such as Windows or Linux.
OSI
Open Systems Interconnection. The seven-layer model used to describe how network communication works.
PA
Posteroanterior. A projection in which the x-ray beam enters the back of the body and exits the front.
PACS
Picture Archiving and Communication System. The system that receives, stores, and displays medical images.
PCI
Peripheral Component Interconnect. The expansion bus that connects cards such as graphics and network adapters.
PDF
Portable Document Format. A fixed-layout document format used for reports and printouts.
PDI
Portable Data for Imaging. The IHE profile for putting studies on CD, DVD, or USB in a standard layout.
PDSA
Plan, Do, Study, Act. A cycle for testing a small change and learning from the result.
PET
Positron Emission Tomography. Nuclear imaging that shows how a tracer is used in the body.
PID
Patient Identification Segment. The HL7 segment that carries the patient's identifiers and demographics.
PIPEDA
Personal Information Protection and Electronic Documents Act. The Canadian federal privacy law for private-sector organizations.
PIR
Patient Information Reconciliation. The IHE profile that fixes demographics for patients imaged before registration is complete.
QA
Quality Assurance. The program of planned checks, records, and sign-offs that keeps a service within its limits.
QC
Quality Control. Checks that confirm images, data, and equipment meet their standard.
QIDO
Query based on ID for DICOM Objects. The DICOMweb service that queries studies, series, and instances over HTTP.
RAID
Redundant Array of Independent Disks. A way to combine drives for speed, redundancy, or both.
RAM
Random Access Memory. The working memory a computer uses for running programs and data.
RBAC
Role-Based Access Control. Permissions are attached to roles, and people are given roles.
RDP
Remote Desktop Protocol. The Windows protocol for controlling a computer remotely, on port 3389.
REM
Radiation Exposure Monitoring. The IHE profile that sends dose records to a registry for tracking.
REST
Representational State Transfer. A style of web service that uses plain HTTP requests to read and change resources.
RFI
Request for Information. A document asking vendors to describe what they offer.
RFP
Request for Proposal. A formal document that states requirements and asks vendors for a full answer and price.
RFQ
Request for Quotation. A request for a price on a clearly defined item.
RIS
Radiology Information System. The system that schedules exams, tracks orders, and holds reports for radiology.
RLE
Run-Length Encoding. A lossless compression that replaces repeats with a count and a value.
ROI
Return on Investment. Net gain divided by cost, shown as a percent.
RPO
Recovery Point Objective. How much recent data you can afford to lose, measured as time.
RTF
Rich Text Format. An editable document format that keeps basic formatting.
RTO
Recovery Time Objective. How long a service can be down before it must be back.
SAML
Security Assertion Markup Language. XML tokens that let an identity provider vouch for a user to another application.
SAN
Storage Area Network. A dedicated network that provides shared block storage to servers.
SATA
Serial Advanced Technology Attachment. A common drive connection for lower-cost disks and solid-state drives.
SBAR
Situation, Background, Assessment, Recommendation. A short structure for communicating a problem clearly.
SCP
Service Class Provider. The DICOM role that offers a service, such as the archive that accepts a store.
SCSI
Small Computer System Interface. A drive and device interface used in enterprise storage.
SCU
Service Class User. The DICOM role that requests a service, such as a modality sending images.
SIIM
Society for Imaging Informatics in Medicine. The professional society for imaging informatics.
SIU
Scheduling Information Unsolicited. The HL7 message family that carries appointment bookings and changes.
SLA
Service Level Agreement. The contract terms for response time, resolution time, and uptime.
SMA
Support and Maintenance Agreement. The contract that covers support, fixes, and upgrades after go-live.
SMB
Server Message Block. The Windows file-sharing protocol.
SNMP
Simple Network Management Protocol. The protocol for polling devices and receiving alerts from them.
SNOMED
Systematized Nomenclature of Medicine. The large clinical terminology of findings, body structures, and procedures.
SOP
Service-Object Pair. A DICOM pairing of a service with an object type, such as CT Image Storage.
SOW
Statement of Work. The document that states exactly what a vendor will deliver and when.
SQL
Structured Query Language. The language used to query and change a relational database.
SSD
Solid-State Drive. A flash storage drive with no moving parts.
SSH
Secure Shell. The encrypted protocol for remote command-line access, on port 22.
SSO
Single Sign-On. One login that gives access to many applications.
STOW
Store Over the Web. The DICOMweb service that stores objects on a server over HTTP.
SWF
Scheduled Workflow. The IHE profile for the order-to-report flow with consistent data across systems.
TB
Terabyte. About one trillion bytes, or 1,000 gigabytes.
TCO
Total Cost of Ownership. Everything a system costs over its life, not just the purchase price.
TCP
Transmission Control Protocol. The reliable, connection-oriented transport used by DICOM, HL7, and HTTP.
TG18
Task Group 18. The AAPM report that defined display test patterns and tolerances for diagnostic monitors.
TG270
Task Group 270. The AAPM report that replaced TG18 for display quality assurance.
TLS
Transport Layer Security. The protocol that encrypts a connection and proves the server's identity.
UDP
User Datagram Protocol. A fast transport with no delivery guarantee.
UID
Unique Identifier. A globally unique dotted number that names a study, series, or object in DICOM.
URL
Uniform Resource Locator. A web address; a launch URL carries the patient and accession to open the right study.
USB
Universal Serial Bus. The connection for peripherals and portable drives.
VDI
Virtual Desktop Infrastructure. Desktops that run in the data center and are shown on a user's screen.
VLAN
Virtual Local Area Network. A logical network created on shared switches.
VM
Virtual Machine. A software-based server that shares physical hardware with others.
VNA
Vendor Neutral Archive. An archive that stores images in standard formats behind open interfaces.
VNC
Virtual Network Computing. A remote desktop tool that shows another computer's screen.
VPN
Virtual Private Network. An encrypted tunnel across an untrusted network.
VR
Value Representation. The DICOM code that says what type of data an element holds.
VUE
Virtual University Enterprises. The name of the testing company that delivers the exam.
WADO
Web Access to DICOM Objects. The DICOMweb service that retrieves objects or rendered images over HTTP.
WAN
Wide Area Network. A network that links sites over long distances.
WBS
Work Breakdown Structure. The project split into smaller pieces of work.
XDS
Cross-Enterprise Document Sharing. The IHE approach to publishing and finding documents across organizations.
XML
Extensible Markup Language. A structured text format that marks data with tags.

The exam itself 22

Certifying body
The American Board of Imaging Informatics (ABII)
Credential
Certified Imaging Informatics Professional (CIIP), for the people who run imaging systems
Questions
170 in all: 130 scored and 40 unscored pilot items. You cannot tell which are which
Time
170 minutes (2 hours 50 minutes), plus 20 more for the tutorial, the non-disclosure agreement, and the survey
Question types
Mostly single-best-answer multiple choice; some select-multiple (4 to 8 options), exhibit or video, and hot-area items
Order
Questions appear in random order, not grouped by domain
Answer rule
You must answer each question before the next one appears; you may flag it and come back
Tools
An on-screen calculator is available
Delivery
A Pearson VUE test center or online with a remote proctor; any day, no testing windows
Attempts
Three attempts within 12 months of being found eligible; postponing does not move the 12 months
Score
Scaled 1 to 99; 75 passes. ABII states the scaled score is not a percentage. A preliminary result shows on screen
Fees
$500 test; $250 retake; $250 re-application after a late cancel; $10 Pearson VUE reschedule fee
Cancel or reschedule
Up to one business day (24 hours) before a test-center appointment, or 30 minutes before an online one; later means reapplying
A missed appointment
Forfeits the fee but does not count as one of the three attempts
Renewal
24 continuing education credits every two years plus an annual renewal fee, with ten-year requirements on top
How the questions read
Informatics scenarios that ask for the FIRST step, the MOST likely cause, or the BEST configuration, document, or recommendation
Total
At least 7 points, and every category minimum met
Experience (minimum 1, maximum 5)
1 point per 12 months as a credentialed imaging professional, a healthcare IT professional, a healthcare informatics professional, or a non-certified radiologic technologist in the military
Academic education (minimum 0, maximum 5)
Highest degree only, not cumulative: 1 for no degree but 30 semester credits (45 quarter); 2 for an associate degree of 60 semester credits; 3 for an associate degree of 90 semester credits; 4 for a bachelor's degree of 120 semester credits; 5 for a master's or doctorate
Imaging informatics degree
1 extra point when the degree itself is in imaging informatics
Continuing education (minimum 1, maximum 4)
1 point per 10 hours of imaging informatics continuing education taken within 18 months of applying
Accreditation
The school must be accredited by a mechanism the United States Department of Education or the Council for Higher Education Accreditation recognizes, or an equivalent authority abroad

DICOM, HL7, IHE, and the codes 91

Information model
Patient, then study, then series, then instance. One patient has many studies, a study has many series, a series has many images or other objects
UID
A globally unique identifier made of numbers and dots, up to 64 characters, built on a root the organization owns. Study, series, and SOP instance UIDs each name one thing and must never repeat for different objects
SOP class
Pairs a service with an object type, such as CT Image Storage. It is the abstract syntax a presentation context proposes
SOP instance
One object of that class, such as a single CT slice, named by its SOP instance UID
SCU and SCP
The service class user asks and the service class provider answers. On a store, the modality is the SCU and PACS is the SCP
{{C-ECHO}}
The DICOM ping: proves the AE titles, address, and port match and an association opens. It does not prove images will flow
{{C-STORE}}
Pushes one object to a provider. Modalities and routers use it to send images to PACS
{{C-FIND}}
Queries a provider at the patient, study, series, or image level and returns matching identifiers
{{C-MOVE}}
Asks a provider to send matching objects to a named destination AE title, which the provider must have configured with an address and port
{{C-GET}}
Retrieves objects back over the same association, so no destination entry is needed
Modality worklist (MWL)
The modality queries the RIS or a broker for scheduled procedures, so demographics are not typed by hand
MPPS
Modality performed procedure step: the modality reports that an exam started, ended, or was discontinued, and which images it made
Storage commitment
The modality asks PACS to take responsibility for stored objects; only after the commitment does the modality delete its local copy
Association
The opening handshake between two AEs: one proposes presentation contexts, the other accepts or rejects each one, data flows, then a release ends it
Presentation context
One abstract syntax (a SOP class) plus the transfer syntaxes the requester can use for it
Transfer syntax negotiation
The two sides agree how the bytes are encoded and compressed. If no proposed syntax is acceptable, that context is rejected and the objects are not sent
Conformance statement
The vendor document listing the SOP classes, SCU and SCP roles, transfer syntaxes, and options a product supports. Read it before buying or connecting a device
DICOMDIR
The index file on portable media that lists the studies on the disc or drive
Implicit VR little endian
1.2.840.10008.1.2: the default every device must support; uncompressed
Explicit VR little endian
1.2.840.10008.1.2.1: uncompressed, each element states its value representation
JPEG lossless
1.2.840.10008.1.2.4.70: compressed with every pixel recoverable
JPEG 2000 lossless only
1.2.840.10008.1.2.4.90: lossless wavelet compression
JPEG 2000
1.2.840.10008.1.2.4.91: may be lossy
JPEG baseline
1.2.840.10008.1.2.4.50: lossy, for review copies
RLE lossless
1.2.840.10008.1.2.5: run-length encoding, lossless
Verification SOP class
1.2.840.10008.1.1: the class {{C-ECHO}} uses
(0010,0010)
Patient's name
(0010,0020)
Patient ID
(0008,0050)
Accession number: ties the images to the order
(0008,0060)
Modality
(0020,000D)
Study instance UID
(0028,0010) and (0028,0011)
Rows and columns, the image matrix
(0028,0100)
Bits allocated per pixel

Information object definitions: what each object contains
Part 4
Service class specifications: store, query, retrieve, worklist
Part 5
Data structures and encoding
Part 6
The data dictionary and the UID registry
Part 7
Message exchange
Part 8
Network communication support
Part 14
The grayscale standard display function
Part 15
Security and system management profiles, including de-identification
Part 18
Web services: {{QIDO-RS}}, {{WADO-RS}}, {{STOW-RS}}
{{QIDO-RS}}
Query (QIDO): find studies, series, or instances over HTTP
{{WADO-RS}}
Retrieve (WADO): fetch objects or rendered images over HTTP
{{STOW-RS}}
Store (STOW): send objects to a server over HTTP
AE title
The name of the application, up to 16 characters and case-sensitive. Each side must list the other's exact AE title
IP address or host name
Where the other device answers. A host name needs working DNS
Port
The listening port. The registered DICOM ports are 104 and 11112; DICOM over TLS is registered on 2762
Unknown AE title
The association is rejected: fix the title on the receiver's allowed list
Wrong port or service down
The connection is refused
A firewall dropping the traffic
The connection times out with no answer
Both directions
Most routes need entries on both devices: the sender needs the receiver's triplet and the receiver needs the sender's title
Message structure
A message is a set of segments, one per line, each ending in a carriage return; segments hold fields separated by a pipe, with components, repeats, and subcomponents set by the delimiters in the first segment
Delimiters
Pipe for fields, caret for components, tilde for repeats, backslash for escapes, ampersand for subcomponents
{{MSH}}
Message header: sending and receiving application and facility, date and time, message type, control ID, version
{{PID}}
Patient identification: the identifier list in PID-3, the name in PID-5, birth date, sex
{{PV1}}
Patient visit: location, class, attending provider
{{ORC}}
Common order: order control and the placer and filler order numbers
{{OBR}}
Observation request: the procedure ordered; the filler order number commonly carries the accession number
{{OBX}}
Observation result: one line of result, such as a line of report text, in OBX-5
ADT
Admit, discharge, transfer: carries patient registration, updates, and merges from the registration system to RIS and PACS
ORM or OMI
Orders: a new, changed, or cancelled imaging order from the order entry system to the RIS
ORU
Unsolicited result: the report text and status from the reporting system to the EMR
SIU
Scheduling: appointments booked or changed
MDM
Medical document management: transcribed or scanned documents and their status
ACK
The acknowledgment. {{AA}} means accepted, {{AE}} means application error, {{AR}} means rejected
MLLP
The framing that carries HL7 over TCP: a start byte (0x0B), the message, then 0x1C and a carriage return. There is no universal port; the registered hl7 port is 2575 and sites often choose their own
Interface engine
Receives, routes, queues, and maps messages between systems. A stalled queue is the first place to look when orders or reports stop arriving
Resources
Small named building blocks of health data, each with its own address and a defined set of fields
REST
Plain HTTPS calls (get, post, put, delete) carrying JSON or XML
Patient
The person
ServiceRequest
The order, such as an imaging request
ImagingStudy
Describes a study, its series, and its instances, and points at the DICOM objects
DiagnosticReport
The report and its status
SWF and SWF.b
Scheduled workflow: order, schedule, acquire, store, commit, and report with consistent data across systems
PIR
Patient information reconciliation: fixes demographics when a patient is imaged before registration is complete, such as a trauma
CPI
Consistent presentation of images: the same grayscale appearance on every display
KIN
Key image note: flags significant images with a comment
PDI
Portable data for imaging: the format for studies on CD, DVD, or USB, with a DICOMDIR
XDS-I.b
Cross-enterprise document sharing for imaging: a registry lists documents, a repository holds them, and a manifest points to the images
IID
Invoke image display: opens the viewer on the right study from another application
REM
Radiation exposure monitoring: sends dose records to a registry for tracking
ATNA
Audit trail and node authentication: central audit logging and encrypted connections between trusted nodes
CT
Consistent time: every system synchronizes its clock to one source so audit trails line up
Integration statement
The vendor's declaration of which IHE profiles and actors a product supports
ICD
Diagnoses and reasons for the exam
CPT
Procedures and billing
SNOMED CT
Clinical terms: findings, body structures, and procedures in a single hierarchy
LOINC
Observations and orders, including many laboratory and imaging order names
RadLex
The radiology lexicon: imaging terms
RadLex Playbook
Standard names and codes for imaging procedures, used to map local procedure names to one set

Modalities, ancillary services, and display QC 17

GSDF
The DICOM grayscale standard display function (Part 14). It maps each pixel value to a luminance so equal steps look equally different on every calibrated display
Just noticeable difference
The smallest luminance change the eye can see; the GSDF spaces its steps by this
AAPM TG18 and TG270
AAPM task group reports on display quality. TG270 replaced TG18 and its test patterns can be used for the same checks
Acceptance test
Done once when the display is installed, with the full set of patterns and measurements
Routine test
Done on a schedule afterward, with simpler checks and a visual pattern
Who performs it
A medical physicist or a trained, supported team. For mammography displays, a qualified medical physicist is required before clinical use
Ambient light
20 to 40 lux recommended for image interpretation
Maximum luminance
At least 250 cd/m2 for general grayscale displays, with 350 or more common for primary reads; mammography displays need more, about 420 to 450
Contrast ratio
Maximum luminance divided by minimum: above 250 for a diagnostic display and above 100 for a clinical one
Contrast response
Within 10 percent of the GSDF
Luminance uniformity
Measure the four corners and the center; they should not differ by more than 30 percent
Matching displays
The centers of the monitors at one workstation should not differ by more than 10 percent
Pixel dropout
Dark specks in a white field that stay put; compare with the manufacturer's allowed amount
Noise check
A low-contrast dot pattern viewed at 30 cm: on a primary diagnosis display all dots are found in three of four quadrants, on others in two of four
Internal photometer check
Compare the internal sensor to an external meter at acceptance and every 10,000 backlight hours
Bit depth
At least 8 bits of luminance resolution
Do not guess from a clean image
A display can drift out of calibration with no visible fault; the test pattern and meter are the evidence

Image management 50

Ergonomics
Adjustable chairs with lumbar support, desks with adjustable height, comfortable keyboards and mice, and monitors set at a comfortable height and angle to cut neck and eye strain
Ambient light
Dim, even, and controllable at each work area; 20 to 40 lux for reading; avoid glare and reflections on screens
Room layout
Workstations placed so no window or lamp reflects in a screen, with room to move and to consult
Noise
Absorb it with panels and carpeting, and isolate dictation users from each other
Temperature and air
Many computers warm a room, so plan airflow and cooling for each workstation
Monitor positioning
Matched displays side by side with the same luminance and calibration
Human-computer interface
The integration of the EMR (also called the EHR), RIS, PACS, and the reporting tool; input devices such as mice, keyboards, and dictation microphones; display devices
Hanging protocol or display protocol (Workflow term)
The rules that decide how images are arranged on the screen for a given exam type, so the radiologist does not rearrange each study
Read-ready (Workflow term)
The state when all images and priors have arrived and the study is complete enough to be read
Postprocessing and 3D (Workflow term)
Reformats, multiplanar views, and rendering built from the stored slices
Key images and annotations (Workflow term)
Selected images and marks that point out what matters, stored as their own objects
Priors and relevant-prior rules (Workflow term)
The rules that fetch earlier exams of the same patient and body part for comparison
Teaching files (Workflow term)
Cases kept for education, which must be de-identified
Remote interpretation (Workflow term)
Teleradiology and telehealth reads from another site, which depend on bandwidth and a secure connection
Workflow optimization (Workflow term)
Routing, worklists, and protocol rules that put the right study in front of the right reader
Lossless
Every pixel is recovered exactly. Typical reduction is about 1.8 to 2.8 times, and storage planners often use 2.5 to 1
Lossy
Some data is permanently discarded. Typical ratios used when interpreting are about 20 to 1 for radiography, 10 to 1 for CT, and 5 to 1 for MRI
Who decides
The radiology department and its policies choose what may be lossy-compressed for interpretation; it is not a decision for IT alone
The ratio on the image
A lossy ratio must be stated on each image of the study
Lossy for review
Fits web distribution and review copies better than primary interpretation
Never lossy under local policy
Mammography images kept as the legal record; lossy compressed mammograms cannot serve as the legal record
The size formula
Compressed size equals original size divided by the ratio
Technologist exam QC
Image count in PACS matches what was acquired; demographics, laterality, and procedure are right
Order reconciliation
Matches each study to its order using the accession number
Storage commitment
Confirms PACS accepted responsibility before the modality deletes its copy
Modality worklist
Prevents typing errors by pulling demographics from the RIS
Merge
Combines two records created for one patient, usually by correcting the ID
Split
Separates one record that holds two patients
Move
Relocates a series or study to the correct patient
The unverified or broken study queue
Holds studies that cannot match an order or patient; someone must own and empty it daily
Audit of every correction
Every merge, split, and move is logged with who and why
Preliminary
An early read, not yet signed as final
Final
The signed report of record
Addended
A final report with an added note; the original text stays
Corrected
A final report replaced because of an error, flagged so readers know
Structured report
Standard fields and terms, easier to search and count
Narrative report
Free text, flexible but harder to analyze
De-identification (Research and sharing)
Remove the 18 identifier types the HIPAA Safe Harbor method lists: names, locations smaller than a state, dates, and ID numbers, among others
Identifiers in an image file (Research and sharing)
Patient name, ID, birth date, accession number, institution, physician names, and private tags
Burned-in annotations (Research and sharing)
Text drawn into the pixels survives header cleaning and needs pixel-level removal
Face reconstructions (Research and sharing)
Head CT and MRI volumes can be rendered into a recognizable face
Pseudonymization (Research and sharing)
Replaces identifiers with a code and keeps a separate key, so the link can be restored by those allowed
UIDs (Research and sharing)
Replace them consistently so a study keeps its own structure without exposing the original
Teaching files (Research and sharing)
De-identify before saving or sharing
CD import
Load the disc, reconcile demographics to the right patient and order, and fix mismatches before the study joins the archive
PDI media
Standard layout with a DICOMDIR; a viewer is often included
Cloud image exchange
Sharing through a network service, usually with the sender pushing or the receiver pulling a study by link or query
XDS-I.b
A standard way for enterprises to publish and fetch imaging documents
Export rules
Policy decides who may export, what is exported, and how it is logged and tracked
Imported study risk
Wrong demographics, duplicate UIDs, unknown transfer syntaxes, and corrupt files

Storage, networks, hardware, identity, data 100

DAS
Direct-attached storage: drives attached to one server; simple, not shared
NAS
Network-attached storage: shared files over the network using SMB, CIFS, or NFS
SAN
Storage area network: shared block storage over a dedicated fabric using Fibre Channel or iSCSI
SSD
Solid-state drive: flash, no moving parts, very fast reads and low latency; used for the active tier and databases
Object storage
Data stored as objects with IDs and metadata, reached by an interface like S3; scales widely and fits long-term archives
Block, file, and object
Block is raw volumes for databases and servers; file is folders and shares; object is flat keyed storage
iSCSI
Block storage over ordinary TCP and Ethernet
Fibre Channel
Block storage over its own fast fabric
SATA and SCSI
Drive interfaces; SATA for lower-cost drives, SCSI for enterprise storage
SMB and CIFS
The Windows file-sharing protocol
NFS
The Unix and Linux file-sharing protocol
S3
The common object storage interface; cloud archives use it
Online
Fast storage holding current and recent studies
Nearline
Slower storage for older studies, still retrievable on demand
Offline
Media taken out of the system, retrieved by hand
Tiering
Moves studies between tiers by age and use
IOPS
Input and output operations per second: the number of reads and writes a storage system sustains; a database needs high IOPS
Replication
Copying data to another system or site as it changes
Mirroring
Writing the same data to two drives or arrays at once
Snapshot
A point-in-time view of a volume used to roll back quickly; it is not a backup on its own
Cloud storage
Rented capacity; check egress costs, retrieval time, and who holds the encryption keys
VNA
A vendor neutral archive stores images in standard formats behind open interfaces so one archive serves many systems and a change of PACS does not mean a data migration
RAID 0 (Usable capacity and failure tolerance)
Striping: all n drives are usable and a single failure loses everything
RAID 1 (Usable capacity and failure tolerance)
Mirroring: usable capacity is n divided by 2; survives one failure per mirror pair
RAID 5 (Usable capacity and failure tolerance)
Striping with single parity: usable is (n minus 1) drives; at least 3 drives; survives one failure
RAID 6 (Usable capacity and failure tolerance)
Striping with double parity: usable is (n minus 2) drives; at least 4 drives; survives two failures
RAID 10 (Usable capacity and failure tolerance)
Mirrored pairs then striped: usable is n divided by 2; at least 4 drives; survives one failure per pair
Worked example (Usable capacity and failure tolerance)
Eight 4 TB drives give 32 TB for RAID 0, 28 TB for RAID 5, 24 TB for RAID 6, and 16 TB for RAID 1 or RAID 10
RAID is not a backup (Usable capacity and failure tolerance)
It survives a failed drive, not deleted files, corruption, a fire, or ransomware
OSI layer 7, application (What to remember)
HTTP, DICOM, and HL7 messages
OSI layer 6, presentation (What to remember)
Encoding and encryption, such as TLS
OSI layer 5, session (What to remember)
Starts, keeps, and ends a conversation, such as a DICOM association or a remote desktop session
OSI layer 4, transport (What to remember)
TCP and UDP, with port numbers
OSI layer 3, network (What to remember)
IP addresses and routers
OSI layer 2, data link (What to remember)
Ethernet frames, MAC addresses, switches, and VLANs
OSI layer 1, physical (What to remember)
Cables, fiber, and radio
TCP (What to remember)
Connection-oriented and reliable, with acknowledgment and retransmission; DICOM, HL7, and HTTP use it
UDP (What to remember)
Connectionless and fast with no delivery guarantee; used by DNS lookups, time, and logging
Hub, switch, router, gateway (What to remember)
A hub repeats everything; a switch forwards by MAC address; a router moves traffic between networks by IP address; a gateway translates between different protocols or networks
Trunk (What to remember)
A link that carries several VLANs between switches
Cat 5e and Cat 6 (What to remember)
Copper cable: gigabit Ethernet to 100 meters; Cat 6 also does 10 gigabit over shorter runs
Fiber (What to remember)
Light through glass: longer distance, no electrical noise; multimode for short runs, single-mode for long
LAN and WAN (What to remember)
A local network in one site versus a network linking sites
VLAN (What to remember)
A logical network on shared switches, used to separate devices such as modalities from office computers
VPN (What to remember)
An encrypted tunnel across an untrusted network
DNS (What to remember)
Resolves names to IP addresses; many AE title and viewer problems are really DNS problems
ARP (What to remember)
Resolves an IP address to a MAC address on the local network
NAT (What to remember)
Translates private addresses to a public one; a modality behind NAT may not be reachable for a {{C-MOVE}}
DHCP (What to remember)
Hands out addresses automatically; give modalities and servers fixed or reserved addresses
Firewall and TLS (What to remember)
A firewall allows or blocks by rule; TLS encrypts a connection and proves the server's identity with a certificate
DICOM (Common port)
104 or 11112 (registered); 2762 for DICOM over TLS
HL7 over MLLP (Common port)
Site-chosen; 2575 is the registered hl7 port
HTTP (Common port)
80
HTTPS (Common port)
443
SSH (Common port)
22
RDP (Common port)
3389
LDAP (Common port)
389
LDAPS (Common port)
636
DNS (Common port)
53
SNMP (Common port)
161 for polling, 162 for traps
Bits and bytes (Rule)
1 byte is 8 bits. File sizes use bytes; link speeds use bits per second
Transfer time (Rule)
Time in seconds equals size in bits divided by link speed in bits per second
Worked example (Rule)
A 262 MB multi-slice CT is about 262 x 8 = 2,096 megabits. On a 1 Gbps link (1,000 megabits per second) that is about 2.1 seconds at best; on a 100 Mbps link it is about 21 seconds
Real throughput (Rule)
Always lower than the link speed because of protocol overhead, shared links, and slow disks; a plan should leave headroom
Prefixes (Rule)
Kilo, mega, giga, and tera step by 1,000 for speeds; storage sellers use 1,000 and operating systems often report 1,024
CPU
Runs instructions; matters for servers, compression, and database queries
GPU
Graphics processor; matters for 3D rendering and for the displays at a reading workstation
RAM
Working memory; a workstation viewing large studies needs plenty
Drives
SSD for speed and hard disks for capacity
NIC
Network interface card; a slow or duplex-mismatched one slows image loading
Buses
PCI Express for cards, USB for peripherals, SCSI for drives
Server roles
Database, image archive, web viewer, interface engine, and application servers
Workstation roles
Diagnostic reading, clinical review, technologist QC, and administration
OS
Windows, Linux, and mobile systems; versions must match what the vendor supports
Runtimes
Applications often need a particular {{.NET}} or Java version
Browser
Web viewers need a supported browser version
RDP and VNC
Remote desktop tools; use them over a VPN and with access controls
VM
A virtual machine: one physical server running several isolated servers
VDI
Virtual desktop infrastructure: desktops hosted in the data center and shown remotely
Mobile devices
Phones and tablets need device management, encryption, and a lockable app
Active Directory
The Microsoft directory holding users, groups, and computers
LDAP and LDAPS
Protocol to query a directory; LDAPS is the encrypted version
Group policy
Pushes settings to computers and users from the directory
SSO
Sign in once to reach many applications; Kerberos does it inside a Windows domain
SAML
XML tokens that let an identity provider vouch for you to another application
OAuth 2.0
Delegated authorization: an app gets a token to act for you without your password
Two-factor authentication
Something you know plus something you have, such as a code on a phone
RBAC
Role-based access control: permissions attach to roles, and people hold roles
{{SELECT}}
Chooses the columns to return
{{WHERE}}
Filters rows by a condition
{{JOIN}}
Combines rows from two tables on a matching key
{{GROUP BY}}
Groups rows so a count or sum is computed per group
Primary key
A column that uniquely identifies a row, such as an accession number in an exam table
Foreign key
A column that points to another table's primary key
Normalization
Splitting data into related tables so each fact is stored once
Index
A structure that speeds up searches on a column; too many slow writes
SQL
The language used to query and change a relational database
CSV
Plain text with comma-separated values; easy to export and open
XML and JSON
Structured text formats for exchange; JSON is lighter
RTF and PDF
Formatted document formats; RTF is editable, PDF is fixed for viewing

Systems management 72

Study size
Images x rows x columns x bytes per pixel. A 512 x 512 CT slice at 2 bytes is 524,288 bytes; 60 slices come to about 31.5 million bytes
Annual storage
Exams per year x average study size. Add imports, growth, and a second copy
Worked annual example
100,000 general radiology studies a year need about 4.1 TB uncompressed: radiography 64 percent at 42 MB, CT 20 percent at 52 MB, MRI 5 percent at 39 MB, ultrasound 5 percent at 18 MB, nuclear medicine 3 percent at 1.3 MB, angiography 3 percent at 15 MB
Compressed size
Original size divided by the ratio. A 4.1 TB year at 2.5 to 1 lossless is about 1.6 TB
Transfer time
Size in bits divided by link speed in bits per second
Downtime per year
(1 minus availability) x 525,600 minutes
Availability
Uptime divided by total time
99 percent
5,256 minutes, about 87.6 hours
99.9 percent
525.6 minutes, about 8.8 hours
99.99 percent
52.56 minutes
99.999 percent
5.256 minutes
Reading the number
Each extra nine cuts allowed downtime to a tenth and costs much more. Check whether planned maintenance counts
Subscription
Pay on a recurring basis; stops working or loses support if you stop paying
Perpetual
Pay once and own the license; support and upgrades are bought separately
Enterprise
One license covers the whole organization
Concurrent
Counts how many people use it at the same time
Named user
Counts specific people no matter when they log in
Per study
Cost rises with exam volume
Test strategy
What will be tested, by whom, in what order, and what counts as a pass
Environment
A test system separate from production, with the same interfaces
Test data
Fake or de-identified patients; never real data in a test system without the same protections
Testers
A mix of administrators, technologists, and radiologists who do the real work
Unit test
One component works alone
Functional test
A feature does what the specification says
Integration test
Two or more systems exchange data correctly
Workflow test
A real scenario runs from order to report
Regression test
Old features still work after a change
User acceptance test
Users confirm the system does their job; sign-off follows
Stress and scalability test
Behavior under heavy load or growth
Security test
Weak passwords, open ports, and access control checks
Test cases, scripts, suites, results
A case is one check; a script is the steps; a suite is a group; the results are recorded for the sign-off
Redundant components
Duplicates of parts such as power supplies, drives, and network cards
HA
High availability: a design that keeps service running through a failure
Clustering
Several servers acting as one so another takes over
Load balancing
Spreads requests across servers
Failover and failback
Failover moves service to the backup; failback returns it to the primary after repair
Synchronous replication
A write is not finished until both copies have it: no data loss, but it needs a fast link
Asynchronous replication
The primary does not wait; the copy lags and a failure can lose the most recent data
RPO
Recovery point objective: how much data you can afford to lose, measured as time
RTO
Recovery time objective: how long you can be down before service must be back
BC and DR
Business continuity keeps the work going while systems are down; disaster recovery restores the systems
Downtime procedures
Written steps for paper, local copies, and re-entry
Downtime viewer
A read-only copy of recent images and reports available when the main system is down
Incident reporting
A ticket system with a priority, owner, and a record of what was done
Dashboards
A live view of the interface queues, storage, and server health
Alerts
Notices on a threshold, such as storage at 80 percent or a stalled queue
SNMP
A protocol for polling devices and receiving traps
Log aggregation
Collecting logs in one place to search across systems
Protocol analysis
Capturing network traffic to see exactly what was sent
DICOM simulators and validators
Tools that mimic a modality or PACS and check files and messages against the standard
Scope
Which systems, years, and data types move
Push and pull
Push: the old system sends; pull: the new one asks
Big-bang versus phased
Everything at one cutover, or in stages with parallel running
Prefetch
Loading likely-needed priors onto the new system before cutover
Physical transfer
Shipping drives when the network is too slow
Data cleanup and standardization
Fixing patient IDs, names, and procedure names before or during the move
Proprietary data and conversion
Annotations, key images, and reports in a vendor format may need conversion or may not move
Validation and reconciliation
Compare counts by patient, study, series, and image between old and new, and sample images
Cost and user impact
Plan for temporary slowdowns, extra storage, and training
Progress reports
Studies moved, studies failed, and estimated completion
HIPAA privacy rule
Governs use and disclosure of protected health information
HIPAA security rule
Requires administrative, physical, and technical safeguards for electronic information
HITECH
Extends HIPAA and sets breach notification duties
GDPR
European privacy regulation with strict consent and data-subject rights
PIPEDA
Canadian federal privacy law for private-sector organizations
Practice parameter
The joint ACR, AAPM, and SIIM document on electronic practice of medical imaging
NIST
The United States standards body whose frameworks guide security controls
Physical security
Locked server rooms, badge access, and screen privacy
System and network security
Patching, hardening, segmentation, and firewalls
Endpoint and application security
Antimalware, least privilege, and secure application settings
Encryption
At rest on disks and backups, and in transit with TLS
Audit trails
Record who opened which record and when; review them for snooping

Operations 31

Philosophy
Improve the process, not blame the person; measure, change, and measure again
PDSA
Plan, do, study, act: a small test of change repeated in cycles
Six Sigma DMAIC
Define, measure, analyze, improve, control: a data-driven method to cut defects
Lean
Remove waste such as waiting, extra steps, rework, and unused talent
SBAR
Situation, background, assessment, recommendation: a clear way to communicate a problem
Fishbone chart
Cause-and-effect diagram that groups possible causes
Pareto chart
Bars ranked by size; a few causes make most of the problem
Run chart and control chart
A run chart shows a measure over time; a control chart adds limits to tell normal variation from a real change
HIPAA
Privacy and security of protected health information
HITECH
Breach notification and stronger enforcement
MQSA
The federal mammography law: facility accreditation, qualified reading physicians, and record keeping
Radiation dose tracking
Collect dose data from each exam and compare it to reference levels
Uptime
Percent of time the system was available
Capacity used and remaining
Storage and growth rate, giving months until full
Exceptions and broken studies
Studies stuck in verification, unmatched, or failed
Unread exams
Exams waiting past the target time
Lost studies
Studies sent but never found
Report turnaround
Time from exam complete to final report
Interface queue depth
Messages waiting to be delivered; a growing queue means a stalled interface
Pivot table
Summarizing a long list by categories, such as exams by modality and month
Bar chart
Comparing amounts across categories
Line chart
A trend over time
Scatter plot
The relationship between two measures
Dashboard
Many live measures on one screen for monitoring
SOW
Statement of work: exactly what the vendor will deliver, when, and who does what
SMA
Support and maintenance agreement: what is covered after go-live and what it costs
SLA
Service level agreement: response times, resolution times, and uptime guarantees, and what happens if missed
Response versus resolution
Response is when they begin; resolution is when it is fixed
Contract renewal
Review terms, price increases, and need before the date; auto-renewal can lock you in
EOSL
End of service life: the date the vendor stops supporting the product, which forces an upgrade or replacement
Operational budget
The recurring cost to run a system: support, licenses, storage growth, and staff

Procurement and project management 31

Justification
Why the organization needs it, supported by total cost of ownership and return on investment
TCO
Everything the system costs over its life: purchase, installation, licenses, hardware, storage, support, staff, training, and migration
ROI
Return on investment: (gain minus cost) divided by cost, as a percent. Spending 200,000 to gain 250,000 over five years is 25 percent
Payback period
Initial cost divided by annual net benefit. 200,000 divided by 50,000 a year is 4 years
Goals, scope, and budget
Written down and agreed first; a preliminary budget comes before bids
Procurement policy and governance
The organization's rules for buying and who decides
The plan
Milestones and dates for the whole selection
Needs assessment
Collect, document, analyze, prioritize, and validate requirements with the users
RFI
Request for information: learn who the vendors are and what they offer
RFP
Request for proposal: detailed requirements and a request for a full answer and price
RFQ
Request for quotation: a price for a clearly defined item
Scripted demonstration
Every vendor performs the same scenarios so they can be compared fairly
Reference calls and site visits
Talk to current customers of the same size and type
Scoring matrix
Weighted criteria with scores for each vendor, filled in by all evaluators
Selection
Pick on the scored evaluation and the references
Contract development and negotiation
Define deliverables, acceptance, support terms, price, and exit rights before signing
Goals and scope
What the project will and will not do
Scope change control
Every added request is reviewed for cost, time, and risk and approved or declined
Risks
Internal ones come from within the project; external ones come from outside it
Risk register
A list of each risk, its likelihood, its impact, its owner, and its mitigation
Dependencies
A task that cannot start until another finishes
WBS
Work breakdown structure: the project split into smaller pieces of work
Resources and effort estimates
Who is needed and how many hours each task will take
Milestones
Points that mark a major result
Critical path
The longest chain of dependent tasks; a delay there delays the whole project
Gantt chart
A timeline bar chart of tasks and dependencies
Time-and-task tracking
Recording the real hours against the estimates
Status report
Reports budget, schedule, resources, and quality on a regular basis
Go-live
The cutover to production use
Retrospective
A review of what went well and what did not
Lessons learned
Written after go-live so the next project benefits

Communications and training 33

CMIO
Chief medical informatics officer: a physician who leads clinical systems use
CIO
Chief information officer: leads IT for the organization
Department chair
Leads a clinical department
Section chief
Leads a subspecialty section within a department
Attending
The senior physician responsible for the patient and the report
Resident and fellow
Physicians in training; residents are earlier in training than fellows
Technologist
Performs the exam and checks its quality
PACS administrator
Runs the imaging systems day to day
Informaticist
Designs workflows and connects clinical and technical staff
Anatomical planes
Axial divides top from bottom, coronal divides front from back, sagittal divides left from right
Directional terms
Anterior is front, posterior is back, superior is up, inferior is down, medial is toward the midline, lateral is away from it
Projections
AP: front to back; PA: back to front; lateral: side; oblique: at an angle
Body positions
Supine on the back, prone on the stomach, upright, decubitus lying on a side
Laterality
Right or left side; getting it wrong is a serious data error
Modality-specific terms
Slice, series, sequence, view, and phase mean different things in different modalities
Who
The affected users and owners
What
What is changing, and the effect on workflow
When
The start, the length, and the end
Why
The reason, in the user's terms
How
What users must do differently, and who to call
By role
Radiologists, technologists, clerks, and clinicians need different messages
Notification channels
Email, banner on the login screen, huddles, intranet, and phone for urgent cases
Timing
Give notice early enough to plan, and send reminders before and after
Downtime and upgrade notices
State the duration, what to use meanwhile, and what to do when it ends
Needs assessment triggers
A new system, a workflow change, or a system upgrade
Audience
Size, location, and role decide the method
Instructional objectives
What the learner can do afterward, stated so it can be checked
Delivery settings
In person or virtual
Presentation
Written guides, graphics, and video
E-learning
Self-paced modules that scale to a large audience
Super-users
Trained staff in each area who coach colleagues and report issues
Assessment
A quiz tests knowledge, observation checks the task, a survey gathers opinion
Task analysis
Break a job into steps to see where people fail
